 1           Gen Digital, Inc. (“Gen Digital” or “Plaintiff”) alleges, for its complaint (“Complaint”)

 2   against Defendants Sycomp, A Technology Company, Inc. (“Sycomp”) and North American

 3   Systems International, Inc. (“NASI”) (together, “Defendants”), as follows:

 4                                  NATURE OF THE COMPLAINT

 5           1.      This Complaint arises from Defendants’ failure to fulfill their contractual

 6   indemnity obligations to Gen Digital, the entity formerly known as Symantec Corporation

 7   (“Symantec”), to indemnify Symentec pursuant to a Product Purchase Agreement (“PPA”)

 8   between Symantec and Sycomp, and pursuant to a Service Delivery Agreement (“SDA”)

 9   between Symantec and NASI. Defendants have also failed to fulfill their contractual indemnity

10   obligations to Gen Digital pursuant to an agreement between Symantec, on the one hand, and

11   Defendants, in partnership and TERiX Computer Company, Inc. (“Terix”), on the other hand.

12   to provide certain software maintenance, updating, and patching services for Symantec’s

13   computer servers (the “Solaris Patching Agreement”), which services infringed the copyrights

14   of a third party.

15           2.      In a separate lawsuit, Plaintiff DXC Technology Company (“DXC”), as

16   successor-in-interest to Hewlett Packard Enterprise Services (“HPES”) (itself the successor-in-

17   interest to Electronic Data Systems Corporation (“EDS”)), has alleged that Gen Digital (f/k/a

18   Symantec), has certain contractual indemnity obligations—arising from HPES’s work in

19   connection with the same software maintenance, updating, and patching services—which

20   remain unfulfilled. In that lawsuit, Gen Digital alleges that, to the extent it has any indemnity

21   obligations to DXC, those obligations should be satisfied in full by Sycomp and NASI,

22   pursuant to valid and enforceable indemnification provisions in their agreements with Sycomp

23   and NASI, which encompass the services provided to Symantec by the Sycomp/NASI/Terix

24   partnership.

25                                               PARTIES

26           3.      Plaintiff Gen Digital is a corporation duly organized and existing under the laws

27   of the state of Delaware. Its principal place of business is located at 60 E. Rio Salado Parkway,

28   Suite 1000, Tempe, Arizona 85281.

 2 corporation duly organized and existing under the laws of the state of Delaware and with its

 3 principal place of business located at 350 Ellis Street, Mountain View, California 94043.

 5   Symantec.

 7   of the state of California. On information and belief, Sycomp’s principal place of business is

 8   located at 50 Tower Lane, Suite 1785, Foster City, California, 94404.

 9           7.      Defendant NASI is a corporation duly organized and existing under the laws of

10 the state of Minnesota. On information and belief, NASI’s principal place of business is

11   located at 875 Blue Gentian Road, Suite 400, Eagan, Minnesota, 55121.

12                                   JURISDICTION AND VENUE

13           8.      This Court has subject matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. §1332 because the
14   matter in controversy exceeds $75,000, exclusive of interest and costs, and is between citizens
15   of different States.
16            9.      Personal jurisdiction over Sycomp and NASI and venue are proper because the
17   relevant agreements between Symantec and both Sycomp and NASI provide that any legal
18   action arising under those agreements shall be brought in the state or federal courts located in
19   Santa Clara County, California, that the parties consented to such personal jurisdiction and
20   venue therein, and also because a substantial part of the events that give rise to this lawsuit
21   occurred in Santa Clara County, California, within this District.
22                                     GENERAL ALLEGATIONS
23           A.      The Parties’ Contractual Relationships
24           10.     In 2007, Symantec outsourced its IT maintenance to Electronic Data Systems
25   (“EDS”), which was acquired by Hewlett Packard (“HP”) in 2008. As part of its services to
26   Symantec, HP maintained Sun Microsystems (“Sun”) branded devices running the Solaris
27   operating system. These services included updating the software and installing software
28   patches. Eventually, the HP entity that provided IT maintenance services to Symantec became
                                                     3

 1   known as Hewlett Packard Enterprise (“HPE”), which services were eventually performed by

 2   HPE’s services division (“HPES”).

 3          11.     In 2008, Symantec and HPES entered into an Information Technology Services

 4   Agreement (“the ITSA Agreement”). The ITSA Agreement provided that Symantec had

 5   certain indemnity obligations to HPES.

 6          12.     In 2010, Symantec contracted with Sycomp for certain IT services, which

 7   relationship was memorialized by a Product Purchase Agreement, effective September 17, 2010

 8   (the “PPA”).

 9          13.     Section 9 of the PPA relates to Sycomp’s indemnification obligations to

10   Symantec. Section 9.2, entitled “Infringement Indemnification”, provides that:

11          Supplier [Sycomp] shall indemnify, hold harmless and, at Symantec’s request, defend
            Symantec and its officers, directors, employees, partners and clients from any claims,
12          losses, liabilities, damages, demands, suits, causes of action, judgments, costs or
            expenses (including court costs and any reasonable legal fees) arising from any claims
13
            that any Product, Services and/or any Developments prepared or provided by or on
14          behalf of Supplier hereunder infringe or misappropriate the IPR [intellectual property
            rights] of any third party.
15

16   (PPA, §9.2.)
17          14.     Section 9.3 of the PPA, entitled “Indemnification Procedures”, provides that:
18          Symantec will promptly notify Supplier [Sycomp] of Symantec’s receipt of any service
            of process of any such claim giving rise to Supplier’s indemnification obligations (but
19          any delay by Symantec in giving such notice shall not be deemed a breach of this
            Agreement and shall not excuse Supplier’s obligations under this Section 9 except to the
20
            extent, if any, that Supplier is materially prejudiced by such delay). Symantec will
21          provide Supplier with reasonable assistance and the opportunity to assume sole control
            over the defense and settlement. Supplier agrees that Symantec, at its own expense,
22          shall have the right to retain its own separate counsel to participate in the defense or
            settlement of any claim. Symantec shall have the right to participate in the defense of
23          any such demand, suit or cause of action concerning matters that relate to Symantec,
24          and that such suit will not be settled without Symantec’s consent, which shall not be
            unreasonably withheld, unless such settlement includes (i) no admission of liability, (ii)
25          a release of all claims against Symantec, and (iii) imposes no obligations on Symantec
            (other than, if applicable, ceasing the use of any Infringing Product or Service). If, in
26          Symantec’s reasonable judgment, a conflict exists in the interests of Symantec and
            Supplier in such demand, suit or cause of action, Symantec may retain its own counsel
27          whose reasonable fees shall be paid by Supplier.
28   (PPA, §9.3.)

 1          15.     In 2010, Sun was acquired by Oracle Corporation (“Oracle”).

 2          16.     In 2012, following Oracle’s acquisition of Sun and its Solaris workstation

 3   operating system, Symantec sought to explore less expensive IT maintenance and support

 4   options for its older Sun-branded devices.

 5          17.     At or about this time, Symantec approached Sycomp, with whom it had

 6   contracted in 2010, regarding potential IT maintenance services as an alternative to Oracle’s

 7   more expensive services. In response to Symantec’s inquiry, Sycomp indicated that it could do

 8   the work itself on a time and materials basis, but such an arrangement may not meet

 9   Symantec’s needs. Accordingly, Sycomp introduced Symantec to NASI.

10          18.     In mid-2012, in connection with exploring these options, Symantec and NASI

11   executed a Service Delivery Agreement, effective August 1, 2012 (the “SDA”). The SDA was

12   signed by Greg Springer, CFO/GM of NASI, on August 9, 2012. The SDA bears the stamped

13   and written signature of Diana Chow on behalf of Symantec.

14          19.     Section 1.1 of the SDA provides:

15            This Agreement defines the obligations and responsibilities of NASI and
              [Symantec] to support [Symantec’s] installed base of desktop and server
16            computer systems.
17   (SDA, §1.1.)

18          20.     Section 1.2 of the SDA provides:

19            It is the understanding of both parties to this Agreement that NASI will be
              entering into a contractual arrangement with a third party to provide the
20
              Services specified under this Agreement (the “Services”) with terms identical
21            to this Agreement (the “Third Party”). NASI agrees that it shall be fully
              responsible and liable to [Symantec] for all acts, omissions and breaches by
22            its Personnel as if the same were undertaken directly by NASI. It is the
              further understanding of NASI and [Symantec] that NASI’s contractual
23            relationship with any Third Party shall in no way modify, limit, or reduce
              NASI’s obligations under this Agreement.
24

25   (SDA, §1.2.)

26          21.     The IT maintenance services provided by NASI—through its

27   “contractual arrangement with a third party”—included various types of hardware and

28   software support defined in Section 2.0 of the SDA.

 7           24.     Symantec’s principal contact at Sycomp was Caron Rakich (“Rakich”), a

 8   Sycomp client executive. Rakich advised Symantec that Sycomp had recently become an agent

 9   for Terix and offered to facilitate a demonstration from Terix, in partnership with NASI, of

10   Terix’s tools and portal. Rakich assured Symantec that “Terix can 100% patch any Sun devices

11   under their support up to Solaris Version 10 at this time.”

12           25.     On February 25, 2013, Rakich sent an email to Lee Buckland (“Buckland”), a

13   service manager at Symantec. Buckland’s responsibilities included managing Symantec’s

14   outsourced IT providers and coordinating ongoing maintenance. In her email, Rakich wrote

15   she was not surprised that Symantec was validating and questioning their Solaris support

16   services. After noting that Sycomp had been through a similar vetting process with other

17   clients, she recommended that Symantec participate in a conference call to address the issues

18   and to explain how Terix provides support. Rakich said that she felt this would be the correct

19   next step in light of Symantec’s concerns.

20           26.     Symantec agreed to this proposal and, on March 12, 2013, Buckland and Paul

21   DeBacker (“DeBacker”), a Symantec IP Vendor Manager, participated in a call with a Terix

22   representative and EVP, Larry Quinn (“Quinn”), to discuss Terix’s purported license rights to

23   provide the services sought by Symantec and offered by the Sycomp/NASI/Terix partnership.

24   In that call, Quinn emphasized that the Sycomp/NASI/Terix partnership had the right to obtain

25   the necessary patches and updates without infringing anyone else’s—namely, Oracle’s—

26   intellectual property rights.

27           27.     After the discussion, Quinn sent Buckland and DeBacker an email thanking

28   them for participating in the call and stating: “I will be completing the transcription and

 4   email to which he attached a twenty-page document entitled “LICENCE/RIGHTS

 6   preprepared content explaining how NASI/Terix were able to legally provide software patches

 9   support scope, and we hope that the process, while lengthy, was valuable for Symantec.”

10   Sycomp and NASI never repudiated, contradicted, or even questioned Quinn’s assertions and

11   proceeded to work with Terix to provide the services.

15   to Symantec/NASI/Sycomp Master Agreement.”

17   Maintenance,” which attached the SDA between NASI and Symantec. In this email, Rakich
18   stated “[a]attached is the fully executed terms and conditions which [Sycomp is] able to operate
19   under with NASI/Terix.”

21   he stated, inter alia, “Hope you are having a good week. Some of our team (NASI and TERiX)
22   had asked that I provide some information on Solaris 8 since Symantec is using this version as
23   well.”

25   Symantec a revised quotation for renewal of maintenance for assorted server and storage
26   equipment for 4/1/14-3/31/15 in the amount of $1,543,934.24. The quotation again explicitly
27   states: “Terms subject to Symantec/NASI/Sycomp Master Agreement.”
28            33.   On April 3, 2013, Symantec issued a purchase order to Sycomp in the amount of

 3          34.       On April 9, 2013, Sycomp, NASI and Terix made a PowerPoint presentation to

 4   Symantec. In that presentation, the three companies again represented themselves as “partners”

 5   and Sycomp and NASI also indicated they were Terix resellers. Sycomp and NASI specifically

 6   represented to Symantec that they were Terix resellers with “[o]ver 10 years of partnership” and

 7   that Sycomp, NASI and Terix had “[h]undreds of clients.” Terix required its resellers (including

 9   Agreement”) in order to resell Terix’s services. The Reseller Agreements provide in part that,

10   “Terix and Reseller enter into this Agreement for the purposes of Reseller offering TERiX

11   Services to Resellers’ customers.” (Emphasis in original.) The Reseller Agreements also provide

12   that “Reseller will receive a commission of 10% (unless negotiated otherwise prior to submission

13   to the customer) on TERiX services sold by the Reseller.”

14          35.       On April 10, 2013, a Terix representative sent an email to Symantec, Sycomp

15   and NASI representatives entitled “Terix Meeting Follow Up.” The email further confirmed

16   the interconnected relationship by beginning with, “Thank you again from Sycomp, NASI and

17   Terix for the new business.”

18          36.       Thus, by April 10, 2023, Symantec, on the one hand, and Sycomp, NASI and

19   Terix, on the other hand, had formed an agreement that was partly oral and partly written, in

20   which Sycomp/NASI/Terix would provide software patches to be installed on Symantec’s

21   Solaris systems (the “Solaris Patching Agreement”). This agreement was explicitly “subject to

22   Symantec/NASI/Sycomp Master Agreement.” The expression “Master Agreement” is a
23   reference to the PPA with respect to Sycomp, and the SDA with respect to NASI. Thus, the
24   Solaris Patching Agreement necessarily included the above-quoted indemnification obligations
25   Sycomp and NASI had to Symantec in the PPA and SDA, respectively.

28   installing patches provided by Terix and there were numerous communications between and

 2          C.      The Demands for Indemnification and the Oracle v. HPES Lawsuit

 3          49.     On July 17, 2015, HPES notified Symantec of Oracle’s intent to file suit against

 4 HPES in relation to Terix’s provision of Oracle/Sun software and support services to HPES

 5   customers, including Symantec. Oracle alleged, inter alia, that Terix provided Solaris patches

 6   to Symantec for older Solaris servers, which HPES then ultimately installed for Symantec, as

 7   well as several other customers, and that such conduct constituted copyright infringement.

 8          50.     On August 21, 2015, Symantec notified Sycomp and NASI of HPES’s

 9   indemnity demand and, in turn, requested indemnification from Sycomp/NASI pursuant to the

10   indemnification provisions of the PPA (between Symantec and Sycomp) and the SDA (between

11   Symantec and NASI).

12          51.     On March 13, 2016, Oracle filed suit against HPES in the U.S. District Court,

13   Northern District of California, captioned Oracle America, Inc., et al. v. Hewlett Packard

14   Enterprise Company, Case No. 3:16-cv-01393-JST (the “Oracle v. HPES Lawsuit”), which

15   included claims for (1) copyright infringement; (2) interference with contract; (3) intentional

16   interference with prospective economic relations; and (4) unfair competition.

17          52.     Thereafter, counsel for Symantec/Gen Digital had multiple communications
